14.2–14.4 Continuity, Partial Derivatives and Tangent Planes

14.2 wraps up with continuity of compositions and limits in more than two variables; 14.3 defines the partial derivatives, their notations, implicit differentiation, higher derivatives and Clairaut’s Theorem; 14.4 starts with the tangent plane and derives its equation.

Added picture (not on the board), drawn to scale for the lecture’s example (Section 6) with frozen at , so . Ticks every 0.5 in and every 10 in . The orange line is the secant through and ; as it turns into the red tangent, slope .

Explanation (added)

The definition says: walk away from in the x-direction only (that is why the -slot stays ), measure the change in , divide by the step , and let the step shrink. It is exactly the Calc I derivative of the one-variable function . Stewart’s Definition 4 (p. 963) is the same with replaced by a general point , which turns and into functions of two variables. In practice you never use the limit: to find , regard as a constant and differentiate with respect to (Stewart’s “Rule for Finding Partial Derivatives”, p. 963).

10Clairaut’s Theorem

Outline HW§14.3 #53 p. 970 · verify Clairaut
Clairaut’s Theorem

Let be a function defined on a disc containing point . If both and are continuous on , then

Explanation (added)

For the functions you meet in this course (polynomials, exponentials, sines, and so on, away from where they blow up) the mixed partials are continuous, so you may compute whichever order is easier. Section 9’s example is an instance: . Stewart states it on p. 967 (proof in Appendix F) and adds that it extends to higher orders, for example when these are continuous.

12The tangent plane

Outline HW§14.4 #11 p. 982 · graph and zoom in

Let be a surface in given by points , where and are continuous. Let be a point in . Let and be curves in given by the intersection of with the planes and , resp. Let , be the tangent lines to , at .

Sketch at the top right: the surface over the axes, the dashed curve and the curve crossing at , their tangent lines and through , and “” underneath.

Definition

The tangent plane to at is the plane containing and .

Turns out (14.6): any curve in passing thru has its tangent line in the tangent plane at .

The tangent plane at is the plane that best approximates the surface at .

Explanation (added)

Two lines through one point that are not parallel determine exactly one plane, so “the plane containing and ” makes sense. Their slopes are the two partial derivatives from Section 6: the line in the plane has slope and the line in the plane has slope . The claim about every other curve through is proved later (§14.6); it is why the tangent plane is the best flat approximation, not just one plane that happens to contain two lines (Stewart §14.4, Figure 1, p. 974).

What a typical exam question looks like
  • Say where a function such as , or is continuous, with a reason (composition of continuous functions; outline HW §14.2 #37, #39).
  • Find and (or all first partials of a function of three or four variables) and evaluate them at a point, like , above (outline HW §14.3 #17, #19, #23, #31, #33).
  • Use the limit definition to find or for a simple function (outline HW §14.3 #65).
  • Interpret and as slopes of traces, or read their signs off a graph (outline HW §14.3 #5; practice widget in Section 6).
  • Estimate a partial derivative from a table of values with a difference quotient, Definition 4 with a small step instead of a limit (outline HW §14.3 #1).
  • Find and by implicit differentiation, sometimes at a given point (outline HW §14.3 #41, #43).
  • Find all second partial derivatives and check that (outline HW §14.3 #47, #49, #53; third-order partials in #59, #63).
  • Find an equation of the tangent plane to at a given point (outline HW §14.4 #1, #5).

Exercise numbers are the course outline’s (Stewart 9th ed., exercises on pp. 960, 969–970 and 981–982). Tests are built from these with the numbers changed and are written without a calculator, so leave answers exact.
